headline: Papua New Guinea families run short of food and water

sources.title: El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a 'national crisis' as rivers dry up and local farms fail (The Guardian)
From drought to deluge: 'Super' El Niño's expanding reach (UN News)
PNG faces crisis due to impacts of El Niño, sends warning to rest of Pacific (PINA)
Starvation fears as water sources dry up (The National)

chunks.text: In the mountains of Papua New Guinea, a Pacific island country north of Australia, many families are [[skipping meals]]. A long [[drought]], a time with very little rain, has {{set in}}. Rivers and [[creeks]] have {{dried up}}. Family [[food gardens]], small farms that grow most of their food, are failing. A manager at a large international [[aid group]] says some families have {{cut back}} to one meal a day.

verbs.correct: To begin and seem likely to last
verbs.wrong: To be measured by weather experts
verbs.why: Winter sets in early in the mountains. Cold weather often sets in by late October. In Papua New Guinea, a long drought has set in.

verbs.correct: To have no water left at all
verbs.wrong: To change direction toward the sea
verbs.why: Small streams dry up every summer. The pond behind our school dries up when it does not rain. Rivers and creeks in Papua New Guinea have dried up.

verbs.correct: To eat or use less than before
verbs.why: When money is short, my family cuts back to one coffee a day. Many students cut back to two meals a day before payday. A manager at a large international aid group says some families have cut back to one meal a day.

chunks.text: The drought is linked to El Niño, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean that changes weather. Some areas have had less than a quarter of their usual rain since August, the Guardian reported on October 30. As many as 8 million people are [[affected]], the weather service says. The UN says 1.2 million people need [[food aid]]. Food prices are {{going up}}. In the high mountains, [[frosts]] have also {{wiped out}} sweet potato crops, officials say.

verbs.wrong: To be sold in local markets
verbs.why: Bus fares go up every January. The price of fruit goes up when the weather is bad. Food prices in Papua New Guinea are going up.

verbs.wrong: To cover plants to keep them warm
verbs.why: A single storm often wipes out a farmer's whole crop. Hungry insects wipe out the corn in some years. In the high mountains of Papua New Guinea, frosts have wiped out sweet potato crops.

chunks.text: One mother says she and her children {{head out}} every afternoon to walk miles for water. Schools and [[health centers]] open for only half a day, a resident says. Without water, some clinics {{turn away}} patients who need overnight care. Rivers are too low for boats, so some [[remote]] villages are {{cut off}}. The capital's electricity is made at [[dams]], and their water is low. So the power company has planned [[blackouts]]. They could {{drag on}} for up to 10 months.

verbs.wrong: To wait in line at a well
verbs.why: We head out at seven every morning. My neighbor heads out to the store after lunch. One mother and her children head out every afternoon to walk miles for water.
The restaurant turns away people without a reservation. The shelter never turns away a hungry person. Without water, some clinics turn away patients who need overnight care.

verbs.correct: To separate a place from others
verbs.wrong: To bring water to a place by boat
verbs.why: Deep snow often cuts off the mountain town in winter. A flood sometimes cuts off our street from the main road. Rivers are too low for boats, so some remote villages are cut off.

verbs.correct: To last longer than people want
verbs.wrong: To start again after a short stop
verbs.why: Long meetings often drag on past dinner time. The rainy season sometimes drags on into June. The blackouts in the capital could drag on for up to 10 months.

chunks.text: The government has [[declared]] a national [[humanitarian crisis]]. It has {{set up}} a [[task force]], a team for one urgent job. It says it approved a [[support package]] of 1.65 billion kina, about 370 million U.S. dollars. The prime minister has told provinces to {{gear up}} for a long [[dry season]]. Churches, [[labor unions]] and business groups have {{spoken out}}. They say there is no clear plan to protect people most [[at risk]].

verbs.why: Many towns set up a special team after a big storm. Schools often set up a club for new students. The government has set up a task force for the drought.
Stores gear up for the holidays in October. Farmers gear up for the harvest every fall. The prime minister has told provinces to gear up for a long dry season.

verbs.correct: To say strongly and publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To collect money for poor families
verbs.why: Some teachers speak out when a school rule is unfair. Doctors often speak out about the dangers of smoking. Churches, labor unions and business groups have spoken out about the drought.

mainIdea.s: A drought linked to El Niño has dried up rivers and family farms across Papua New Guinea. Families now eat less, and schools, clinics and the power supply all struggle without enough water.
mainIdea.why: Rivers and creeks have dried up and food gardens are failing. Some families have cut back to one meal a day, and clinics turn away some patients.

mainIdea.s: Papua New Guinea faces a serious lack of rain, and many villages are short of food and water. Aid groups say officials have done nothing, so churches now lead the whole national response.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the government has declared a crisis and set up a task force. A group of churches and unions has spoken out, saying the plan is not clear.

mainIdea.s: Heavy rain from El Niño has flooded the capital of Papua New Guinea. Thousands of families left their homes as the water rose, and the main airport closed for several days for repairs.
mainIdea.why: Papua New Guinea faces a long drought, not floods. Rivers have dried up, and food prices are going up across the country.

tf.s: Rivers and creeks have dried up in many parts of Papua New Guinea.
tf.why: A long drought has set in, and rivers and creeks have dried up.

tf.s: Some families have cut back to one meal a day.
tf.why: A manager at an aid group says some families now eat only one meal a day.

tf.s: Food prices are going down because of the drought.
tf.why: Food prices are going up, and hard frosts have wiped out some crops in high areas.

tf.s: A lack of water has made some clinics turn away patients.
tf.why: Some clinics turn away patients who need to stay overnight because they do not have enough water.

tf.s: The government has not set up any team to deal with the drought.
tf.why: The government has set up a task force and approved a large support package.

tf.s: A group of churches and business groups says the national plan is very clear.
tf.why: The group has spoken out and says there is no clear plan to protect the people most at risk.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the drought in Papua New Guinea?
A little. That's the island country north of Australia, right?
Right. Rivers and creeks have {{dried up}}, and the family food gardens are failing.
Not much. Some families have {{cut back}} to one meal a day.
And [[as if that weren't enough]], food prices are {{going up}}.
One mother says she and her kids {{head out}} every afternoon and walk miles for water.
Walking that far every day [[is no joke]].
Some clinics even {{turn away}} patients who need to stay overnight. They don't have enough water.
And I complain when my shower is cold. It makes you [[count your blessings]].
In the capital, the blackouts could {{drag on}} for up to ten months.
It declared a crisis and {{set up}} a task force. The prime minister told provinces to {{gear up}} for a long dry season.
But some groups have {{spoken out}}, haven't they?
Yes. Churches, unions and business groups say there's no clear plan. When water is this scarce, a full bucket is [[worth its weight in gold]].
I hope the wet season brings real rain soon.

expressions.def: Used to tell someone to be thankful for the good things they have

expressions.def: Used to say that something is very useful or valuable
